| ~~W3-1~~ | ~~The §5 commerce-API publish path (`/v1/integrations/blackout/commerce/seller/listings/[id]/publish`) can flip an extension listing to PUBLISHED with no signature and no registry row — reject extension-marked listings there or port the bridge~~ — **fixed 2026-09-10 by rejecting.** Porting would mean two copies of a security-critical flow (manifest validation, plugin-slug ownership, duplicate-version-different-artifact check, signing, registry bridge), free to diverge; the seller API remains the only route that can publish an extension, and the commerce route now 409s `extension_publish_unsupported` with a pointer to it. Both markers are covered — `plugin_slug` and a manifest carrying `artifactKind` — via the same `isExtensionListing` predicate the seller route uses, so the two cannot drift on what counts as an extension. **A second defect in the same three lines, not named by this row:** the route stamped `signed_at` while producing no signature, leaving an unsigned listing indistinguishable from a signed one to any later audit. It no longer stamps it. | done | `backend/src/api/v1/integrations/blackout/commerce/seller/listings/[id]/publish/route.ts` |
| ~~W3-2~~ | ~~Signing-key rotation: the publishing-keys document is single-key (derived from the private key); retired-keys support needs an additional env + doc append~~ — **fixed 2026-09-10, and it was a live hazard, not a nicety.** The Blackout client resolves a signature by `keys.find((entry) => entry.keyId === signature.keyId)` and returns `unknown-key-id` on no match (`features/monetization/install/pluginSignature.ts`), so changing `MARKETPLACE_SIGNING_KEY_ID` made **every artifact signed under the previous key refuse to install** — not a warning, a refusal. Rotation was unavailable in practice, which is the same as having no rotation story. The client already treats the document as a keyset, so publishing the retired keys beside the active one was the whole fix on this side. `MARKETPLACE_SIGNING_RETIRED_KEYS` takes a JSON array of `{ keyId, publicKeyPem }` — public keys only; nothing listed there can sign, since `getPrivateKey` remains the only path to a signature. Both key endpoints serve them, active key first so a consumer reaching for `keys[0]` still gets the signing key. A malformed value, a duplicate keyId, or one colliding with the active id **throws** rather than being skipped: dropping an entry would silently stop verifying every artifact signed under it, surfacing as a user's install failing instead of a deploy failing. `assert-env.mjs` requires the active pair alongside it. **W4-4's rotation dependency is now satisfied**; its pre-W4 null-attestation backfill remains open on its own merits. | done | `backend/src/modules/marketplace-signing/service.ts`, `backend/src/modules/marketplace-signing/verify.ts`, `backend/src/api/middlewares/publishing-keys.ts`, `backend/src/api/v1/marketplace/signing-keys/route.ts`, `backend/.env.template` |
| ~~W3-3~~ | ~~`creator_listing.compatible_with` stays dead~~ — **dropped 2026-09-13.** Declared by `Migration20260506300AddPluginThemeFields` as a compatibility map and read by nothing: the column appears in exactly three places repo-wide — the migration that created it, the model that declared it, and the ORM snapshots mirroring the model. Superseded rather than merely unused: compatibility belongs in the signed `manifest`, covered by `manifestHash`, and a second unsigned copy of the same claim is worse than none — whichever a reader trusts, the other can disagree, and the unsigned one is the one an attacker can change. `Migration20260913DropCompatibleWith` drops it; the `down` restores the column but not its contents, because nothing ever wrote any. | done |
| W3-4 | Seller-scoped `plugin:<slug>` entitlement grant is best-effort; `seller_metadata.enabled_extensions` stays authoritative — hardening to authoritative needs a backfill + failure semantics | **deferred (M)** | `backend/src/api/v1/seller/plugins/[slug]/install/route.ts` |

| W3-6 | Cross-repo counterparts — mostly landed same-window: Forge's publish flow consumes the seller surface (Forge W3 G-commits) and Blackout's provider consumes the registry read side (blackout W3 B1). Still open: Blackout featured-vendors client view (homepageCard.to target) + the client's pinned-key flip to the well-known keyset (operator/release item) | **other repos** | blackout `apps/blackout-client` |
| ~~W3-7~~ | ~~**The backend typecheck job cannot catch a whole class of type error.**~~ — **closed 2026-09-13, and the tradeoff was taken.** `Lint & Type Check` now runs `medusa build` before `tsc --noEmit`, so the generated `query.graph` types exist and a bad `RemoteQueryFilters` fails in the fast job instead of surfacing minutes later in `Build backend`. It costs ~35s and duplicates work the Docker build does; worth it, because nothing broken could merge before either — the cost was always signal latency, and latency is what a solo maintainer pays for in context switches. Order matters and is commented in the workflow: `medusa build` excludes `src/**/__tests__/**`, `tsc --noEmit` covers the specs but needs the generated types, so both run in that order. **The blocker turned out to be bigger than the row recorded.** Generating types made `tsc` report `TS2321: Excessive stack depth` — the row named two files; there were **four** (`create-digital-product-order`, `rental/upsert-rental-config`, `complete-cart-with-tickets`, `rental/add-to-cart-with-rental`), because TypeScript caps how many of these it reports per compilation and clearing the first two revealed the rest. One cause: a `useQueryGraphStep` row is typed as the whole generated entity, and any SDK construct consuming it compares `(T | WorkflowData<T>)[]` against `((T | WorkflowData<T>) & T)[]`. Narrowing at the use site does not work — the comparison happens when the reference is *typed*, so clearing it at a `transform` just moved the identical error onto the `WorkflowResponse` two lines down. `workflows/query-rows.ts` holds `asRows<{...}>()` and the whole explanation; the cast is type-only, so wire payloads are unchanged, and the one workflow whose result reaches an HTTP response was checked against its callers first. CONTRIBUTING's matrix is updated. | done |

Re-point the panels, then drop the plugin from `medusa-config.ts` — after checking the `review` table for rows worth migrating | **deferred (L)** | `backend/medusa-config.ts` plugins block; `vendor-panel/src/routes/reviews/` |
| ~~W4-2~~ | ~~karma_event append-only is service convention, not schema enforcement~~ — **enforced 2026-09-13.** `Migration20260913KarmaAppendOnly` installs a trigger refusing UPDATE and DELETE on `karma_event`. W4 had already made each event tamper-*evident* via its attestation; this makes the log tamper-*resistant*, which is the half a hash cannot supply — an attestation tells you a row changed, a constraint stops it changing. Verified against Postgres 16 rather than assumed: INSERT passes, UPDATE fails, DELETE fails, **soft delete fails** (Medusa's delete is an UPDATE setting `deleted_at`, so it is the case that mattered), a counter-event with a negative delta passes, and the `ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER` escape hatch works for a future migration that genuinely needs it. Safe because `service.ts` holds exactly one write, `createKarmaEvents`, with the attestation built before the insert rather than stamped on after — there is no legitimate second write to a row. Corrections keep the shape the model was designed for: append a counter-event, which is itself attested and attributable. | done |

The row becomes live the day an edit or delete path lands, and what it will need then is a compensating **negative** event rather than a mutation — the log is append-only by design, and the existing grant is keyed `(source_module: "reviews", source_id: <review id>)`, so the reversal has to carry its own distinct source id or the dedup index will swallow it. Left open rather than pre-built: a hook for a path that does not exist cannot be tested against the shape that path will have. | **deferred (S), blocked on an edit path existing** | `backend/src/lib/karma-grants.ts`, `backend/src/api/store/reviews/route.ts` |

## ⚠️ Critical: money-path atomicity was silently disabled (FIXED 2026-06-20)

**Severity: high (financial correctness).** Surfaced by the money-path concurrency
soak once it was made runnable in the production-readiness pass.

The "atomic-by-default" balance/counter CAS paths **never engaged in production**.
`HawalaLedgerModuleService.resolvePgConnection()` (and the equivalent in
`creator-attribution`) read `this.container_`, but Medusa's `MedusaService` base
stores the module container as `this.__container__` — `container_` is never set.
So `resolvePgConnection()` always returned `undefined`, and every
`createTransfer` / `createInvestment` / affiliate-counter increment silently fell
back to the **non-atomic read-modify-write** path. Under concurrency that allows
account overdraw and lost pool/counter updates (real money/value integrity risk).

The unit tests that "verified" the atomic feature mocked the same wrong
`container_` property, so they passed and masked the bug.

**Fix (this pass):**
- Corrected the container access to `__container__` in
  `backend/src/modules/hawala-ledger/service.ts` and
  `backend/src/modules/creator-attribution/service.ts` (supports both a
  container `.resolve()` and an awilix cradle, plus a MikroORM-manager-derived
  knex fallback for harnesses that don't register `PG_CONNECTION`).
- Updated the two atomic unit specs to mock `__container__` (they now validate
  the real path).
- The money-path concurrency soak (`hawala-ledger/__tests__/concurrency-soak`)
  now runs against live Postgres and passes 3/3: no overdraw under 150 concurrent
  debits on a 100-balance account, value conservation across bidirectional
  transfers, and exact investment-pool totals under concurrent investments.

**Follow-up to verify:** confirm in a full-app (not module-test) context that
`PG_CONNECTION` resolves so production takes tier-1 (registered knex) rather than
the manager fallback; audit any other module copying the `container_` pattern.

A single repo-wide regression guard `scripts/check-no-console.mjs` (`pnpm check:no-console`, wired into the CI `lint` job) now fails on any bare `console.*` in runtime code, excluding each app's logger file, `backend/src/scripts/**`, and tests. Chosen over three separate ESLint `no-console` rules to keep one mechanism across all three apps and avoid disturbing admin-panel's `--max-warnings 1000` ratchet (LR-1).

| SD-25 | **Trivy's image gate goes red without saying what it found.** `docker-build.yml` runs the scan with `format: 'sarif'` and `exit-code: '1'`, so a failing gate prints `Process completed with exit code 1` and nothing else — the findings exist only in the Code Scanning tab. That is a real cost, not a nicety: on 2026-09-13 the `storefront` and `backend` image scans went red on `main`, and the log could not name the CVE or the package, so triage needed repository access the person reading the log may not have. **Fixed here:** a second `trivy-action` step with `format: 'table'`, `exit-code: '0'` and `if: failure()` prints the findings after the gate trips. It costs nothing on a green run, cannot fail the job (the step above stays the only gate), and uses the same image, severities and ignore file, so the table lists exactly what tripped the gate rather than a wider set. | done |
| ~~SD-26~~ | ~~**The 2026-09-13 image-scan failure is untriaged.**~~ — **root-caused and fixed 2026-09-14, and it was not the CVE that was interesting.** SD-25's table step named it on the first red run after merging: `libpcre2-8-0` 10.42-1 in the backend and storefront images, `CVE-2026-86145` (out-of-bounds write, arbitrary code execution via crafted patterns) and `CVE-2026-89161` (memory corruption in `pcre2_jit_match`), both HIGH, both `fixed` in `10.42-1+deb12u1`. **The fix was already published and the Dockerfiles already tried to apply it.** Every runtime stage ends with `apt-get upgrade -y` (or `apk upgrade libuuid` on the two nginx images) under a comment explaining that the base tag is rebuilt on its own cadence and this closes the window. It never ran: `docker-build.yml` builds with `cache-from/to: type=gha,mode=max`, so that layer is restored from cache on every build and the upgrade executes **once**, when the layer is first created. The images keep that day's package versions permanently while the file claims to be patching them. Confirmed rather than inferred — `10.42-1+deb12u1` is present in the bookworm-security `Packages` index, read directly from the mirror, so `apt-get upgrade` would have installed it had it been allowed to run. **This also explains the shape of the failure**: backend and storefront ship a `node:` runtime and failed; `admin-panel` and `vendor-panel` ship `nginx:alpine` and passed — not because they were safe, but because no current advisory happened to hit their frozen Alpine packages. Same latent defect, all four. **Fixed** with a `SECURITY_REFRESH` ARG declared at the top of each runtime stage and referenced inside the upgrade RUN (BuildKit only invalidates on an ARG that is used), fed a UTC date by CI. Daily rather than per-commit or `no-cache`: per-commit rebuilds the runtime stage on every push for nothing, disabling the cache throws away the dependency and build stages too, and a date bounds the exposure at 24 hours while leaving everything above the runtime stage cached. **The lesson worth keeping** is that a security step inside a cached layer is not a security step, and nothing in the pipeline said so — the Dockerfile comment, the workflow and the scan were each individually reasonable. It took the SD-25 diagnostic to surface a CVE whose fix had been sitting one layer away. | done |

**Node came first, and separately.** pnpm 11 requires Node >= 22.13 while CI pinned `NODE_VERSION: '20'` and all four Dockerfiles pinned `node:20-bookworm-slim`. A first attempt (#787) bumped only pnpm and failed every job with `ERR_UNKNOWN_BUILTIN_MODULE: No such built-in module: node:sqlite`; local verification had missed it because the dev shell runs Node 22. The runtime move is therefore its own commit, verified on Node 22 against the unchanged pnpm 10 lockfile before the package-manager change was layered on.

**The hazard the pnpm upgrade carries.** pnpm 11 stops reading `pnpm.overrides` from `package.json` — 84 of them across 5 roots, nearly all pinning a CVE fix. That case warns. The dangerous case is silent: overrides in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` are ignored **entirely** when `--ignore-workspace` is passed, with no diagnostic, and every CI install passed that flag. Reproduced on a scratch project: `minimatch` resolved to the vulnerable **3.0.0** under the flag despite `overrides: minimatch@3: ^3.1.3`, and **3.1.5** without it — and such a tree still passes Trivy, which reads the lockfile and would report the reverted versions as intended. Migration accordingly: overrides to a per-root `pnpm-workspace.yaml` (each app its own workspace root, which is what makes the flag unnecessary), `--ignore-workspace` removed everywhere, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` added to all four Dockerfile `COPY` lines, and an `allowBuilds` block per root since pnpm 11 makes an unadjudicated dependency build script a hard error (two deliberate refusals: `@medusajs/telemetry`, `@sentry/cli`).

`scripts/check-override-coverage.mjs` (#787) guards exactly this and runs before the Trivy filesystem scan. Verified semantically neutral: only `backend/pnpm-lock.yaml` changed, **1761 packages before and 1761 after with zero version-level changes** — the diff is entirely pnpm 11's peer-resolution key encoding — and lockfiles stayed at `lockfileVersion: '9.0'`. | SD-33 | **Every nested `middlewares.ts` under `backend/src/api` was dead code, and the storefront's hawala client never sent the customer.** Proved against Medusa 2.14.2: `MiddlewareFileLoader.scanDir` checks only `<sourceDir>/middlewares.ts` and does not recurse, and the project is loaded as one source dir (`src`), so the nine nested files — rate limiters, validators and `authenticate()` entries for store hawala, store collective, store mutual-aid, vendor hawala, vendor wellness, admin hawala, admin debug, vendor collective and the restaurant-delivery routes — never ran. The earlier P1-16 note said this left store hawala routes with no customer auth; that was wrong, because the framework already applies *optional* customer auth to all of `/store`, and every store hawala handler that needs an actor already 401s without one. What was actually broken: (1) the declared rate limits never applied (deposit and withdraw were unthrottled); (2) the `/deliveries/:id/*` routes had no auth at all; (3) the storefront hawala client sent neither the publishable key nor the bearer, so no wallet, investment or contribution call ever carried the customer. **Fixed:** the live nested sets are renamed `_middlewares.ts`, imported and spread into the root file (the Mercur pattern); the redundant ones (duplicating framework `/admin` or Mercur `/vendor` auth, or empty) are deleted. Required customer auth is now explicit on wallet, bank-accounts, transactions, deposit and withdraw; public routes stay public by design (the pools listing, guest contributions). Limiters carry the declared budgets — deposit and withdraw 5/min, investments 10/min, bank linking 3/hour, store hawala reads 30/min on the authenticated read routes only (the review found that keying the pools listing by IP would have put every anonymous visitor in one bucket now that storefront traffic arrives from the Next server), vendor hawala writes 5/min, pool creation 10/hour, vendor wellness test 5/min — **for the operator to confirm**. The delivery routes get the auth they declared plus ownership guards that answer `forbidden()` for every refusal, including a new participant guard on `/subscribe` (in practice the surface is closed: restaurant and driver tokens cannot be minted today). A dead copy of the vendor CORS middleware, looser than the live one, is removed. A guard spec walks `src/api` and fails on any nested middlewares file the root does not import, and checks the result against Medusa's real loader. The storefront client now goes through a server action that sends the publishable key and the httpOnly session as a bearer; the review found its first path check could be bypassed with an encoded `..` and turned it into a general bearer proxy, so it now normalises the URL, allowlists methods and validates the query. **Open, for the operator:** the store wallet, deposit, withdraw, bank-account and transaction routes carry no feature flag (`docs/POSTURE_A_COMPLIANCE.md` implies they do); the guest contribution route keeps a pre-existing IP-keyed limiter that now sees one IP for all storefront traffic; any other IP-keyed limiter on a route the storefront reaches through a server action has the same property. **Found, not fixed here:** `POST /store/hawala/bank-accounts/link` trusts a `stripe_customer_id` from the request body without checking it belongs to the signed-in customer; the bank-account list filters by `customer_id` while the model has `owner_id`. | done; limiter budgets confirmed by the operator 2026-10-06; wallet-route flag added (SD-35); bank-link ownership fixed (SD-34) | `backend/src/api/middlewares.ts`, `backend/src/api/**/_middlewares.ts`, `backend/src/api/utils/is-delivery-*.ts`, `backend/src/shared/rate-limiter.ts`, `backend/src/api/__tests__/nested-middleware*.unit.spec.ts`, `storefront/src/lib/data/hawala.ts`, `storefront/src/lib/hooks/useHawalaWallet.ts` |

The route is unflagged and live wherever `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` is set (SD-33 records that the wallet routes carry no feature flag). An order settles once its own money is captured: at placement if it already is (Mercur captures right after placing the order set; some Stripe methods capture at authorisation), on `payment.captured`, or in a new reconciler job (`jobs/hawala-card-order-reconcile.ts`, every 15 min: a settle pass over orders placed in the last 7 days, and a refund pass over card orders settled in the last 180 days, found from the ledger's own purchase legs; oldest first, caps logged with counts). Every card-order movement goes through one entry point under a per-order advisory lock (`lib/card-order-reconcile.ts`), so two refund events, the job and a settlement can never interleave or post against stale reads. A settlement that died after its purchase leg is completed by the reconciler; a purchase leg that is not COMPLETED is never built on (logged for a person). A Medusa-native refund of a WHOLE shared collection (an admin cancel on a Mercur cart) refunds every order on it in full; a partial one that no order's split row accounts for is reported (`unattributed_refund`), never guessed onto a seller. Non-USD card orders are refused. A Stripe Connect direct charge posts nothing; other providers keep the old path; flag off, nothing changes (no extra read). **Proved on a real migrated database** (`integration-tests/http/hawala-card-order-settlement.spec.ts`: real order, payment, seller, split-payment and link modules, the real subscribers and job, the real ledger): $40.00 settles as 4000 cents to the order's real seller with a stored breakdown; capture later settles once; two partial refunds post as two deltas and the second reverses the settlement; cancellation does not double-post; a two-seller Mercur cart settles each order for its own share at capture, before Mercur marks the splits captured; a Mercur split refund reaches only its order; a shared collection with no split rows settles nothing; an admin cancel refunding the whole shared collection reverses every order on it; a partial Medusa-native refund on it is reported and posts nothing; a refund the vendor cannot cover is refused with no leg posted; four partial refunds reverse the fee to the cent; a half-finished settlement is completed and a FAILED purchase is not built on; four concurrent reconciliations post one refund. Every new branch was mutation-checked on the real database. The unit specs mock the same query shapes. **History:** the first version mocked the order read and was adversarially reviewed before commit — the review found the read never worked (SD-39), multi-seller carts would not settle and refunds were not wired; The project's jobs load after the plugins' (`getResolvedPlugins` appends the project last), a job's workflow id is `job-<config.name>`, and both workflow engines replace a schedule registered under the same id (redis: same repeat key; in-memory: `remove` before `schedule`), so FBM's handler is the one that runs. A real-app test runs `job-daily-payouts` through the workflow engine and checks for a write only FBM's job makes. **Flag off:** it hands straight to Mercur's handler (unchanged). The exception is once the ledger rail has sent anything (an IN_TRANSIT request, or a COMPLETED one stamped `rail: stripe_connect`): it then refuses, because Mercur would pay those orders again; rollback after cut-over is a one-way door and needs a person. **Flag on** (`lib/ledger-connect-payouts.ts`), one run at a time (transaction-scoped advisory try-lock): (1) **Who:** sellers with an ACTIVE Mercur payout account whose synced Stripe account is US and USD; anything else is reported, not paid (POSTURE_A rule 4). If it can't be covered, the seller isn't paid that run. (3) **Schedule:** a held seller is skipped. Otherwise `getPayoutOptions`' payable balance (after card processing and refunds owed) of at least $1 is requested through `requestPayout`, which recovers what is owed and refuses a hold again. (4) **Send:** every PROCESSING payout request whose seller can be paid and isn't held, the vendor panel's too, is claimed PROCESSING -> IN_TRANSIT by a conditional UPDATE (exactly one sender wins). | SD-44 | **Stripe's dispute fee was paid out of FBM's Stripe balance with nothing recording who bears it.** SD-43 open item (d). Operator answers 2026-10-07: "the vendor whose order was disputed owes it", recovered like a refund they owe; and, for the separate dispute *countered* fee, "BMC can pay it". **Verified against Stripe's own documentation before building** (docs.stripe.com/disputes/how-disputes-work; support.stripe.com "June 2025 pricing updates for disputes" and "Calculate dispute countered fees"): outside Mexico, and unless a Stripe contract says otherwise, the dispute *received* fee ($15 in the US) is taken when a chargeback opens and never returned, win or lose. An inquiry carries none. A separate dispute *countered* fee ($15) is taken only when a dispute is contested, is returned on a win, and is applied as its own balance transfer, not on the dispute's balance transactions. Third-party write-ups disagree about the received fee; Stripe's page is the one this follows. **Done, behind `FF_CARD_ORDER_LEDGER_V1`.** (1) *Read, not assumed.* `disputeFeeCents` (`lib/card-stripe-sync.ts`) sums `fee` over every balance transaction on every dispute. Stripe lists the withdrawal and any reinstatement on the dispute itself, so a returned fee nets out. USD only. The sync stores it per charge, with the largest amount any one chargeback covered (inquiries excluded, whatever the outcome): `hawala_card_charge_state.dispute_fee_cents` (migration `Migration20261007CardChargeStateDisputeFee`) and `disputed_cents` (`Migration20261008CardChargeStateDisputedCents`, separate because the first had already merged). (2) *Who owes it* (`lib/card-dispute-fee.ts`, from the locked per-order reconcile). A single-order payment: that order's seller. A Mercur cart: only when one chargeback covered the whole charge, and then in proportion to each order's authorised amount on its split row; largest remainder, so the shares sum to the fee to the cent. A *partial* dispute on a cart does not say which order was disputed, and the ruling names the vendor whose order was disputed, so nothing is put on any seller; it is logged for a person, and BMC bears it unless someone assigns it. The same applies to a collection where any order lacks a split row. Within an order, a consignment's consignor and vendor legs are split the same way. It posts whether or not the dispute is still open, and whether or not the order was already refunded (a cardholder can dispute a refunded charge). (3) *Posting.* Each post is the difference from what is recorded (COMPLETED or PENDING), keyed by charge, order, leg, cumulative cents and a sequence: the count of fee rows already written for that charge, order and leg, FAILED ones included. So a repeat posts nothing, a larger fee posts only the difference, and a FAILED attempt is retried under the next sequence rather than handed back. `recordDisputeFee` returns only when its own leg COMPLETED. A share that went down is logged for a person, never reversed. A leg still PENDING after 10 minutes is logged. One charge failing does not stop the others. (4) *The leg.* ADJUSTMENT, `VENDOR_RECEIVABLE` -> the card-processing account, where the ledger already records money Stripe keeps. `metadata.leg = vendor_dispute_fee`, naming the charge, owed by the seller earnings account. It names its order by `reference_id`, never `order_id`, so a refund of the order cannot list or reverse it. *Only the ledger's own writers can write any receivable leg.* The admin manual-transfer route (`POST /admin/hawala/transfers`) forwards caller-supplied metadata and references to `createTransfer`, and a receivable is recognised by its `metadata.leg` tag. With a tag alone, a request could have pushed the receivable down by any amount into the card-processing account (the dispute-fee shape, found by the first adversarial review). A second review found it could also record a card-processing debt against any vendor, out of the card-processing account and collected from their next earnings and payouts. That gap predates SD-44, but SD-44 widened it, because dispute fees enlarge that account's balance, the only bound. A request could also post a recovery. So `createTransfer` now refuses a leg carrying any of the five receivable tags (both shortfalls, both recoveries, the dispute fee) unless the top-level `receivable_leg: true` is set. Only `processRefund`'s shortfall legs, `recoverCardProcessingShortfall` and `recordDisputeFee` set it, and no HTTP route forwards it. The dispute fee also needs `vendor_dispute_fee: {order_id, stripe_charge_id}`, matching what the leg names, and is refused without it whatever its accounts. (5) *What the vendor sees.* A new receivable kind, `dispute_fee` (`card-processing.ts`), repaid to the receivable by the existing machinery: 100% of the next seller credit, then the payout and vendor-payment backstops. It is forgiven 180 days after the fee was recorded, which can trail the chargeback. `getPayoutOptions` reports `dispute_fee_owed`. The payout refusal text names chargeback fees. The vendor panel shows "Chargeback fees owed" and says Stripe does not return the fee even if the dispute is won. *The countered fee: BMC bears it*, never a vendor, and nothing records it in the ledger. It never touches a vendor's money, and the ledger is not BMC's expense book. It does not reach a vendor because Stripe does not report it on the dispute's balance transactions, which is all `disputeFeeCents` reads. That rests on Stripe's documented reporting, not on a live account. **Proved on a real migrated database** (`integration-tests/http/hawala-card-stripe-sync.spec.ts`, 13 dispute-fee scenarios, 23 in the file): owed as soon as the dispute opens, once however often it is re-read, and still owed once won, with the payable balance net of it; the next sale repays it first; a lost dispute refunds the order in full and the fee stays owed; a dispute first seen already lost; a dispute filed after a full refund; a whole-charge dispute on a cart split 857 / 643 of 1500 by 40 / 30; a rising fee posting only the difference (keys `-to-1500-0`, `-to-3000-1`), and a lower one later posting nothing; a FAILED earlier attempt retried under the next sequence; a partial chargeback on a cart put on no seller (a cart with no split rows never settles, so nothing posts; the attribution refusal for a cart where any order lacks a split row is proved in the unit spec); the fee shape refused when written with caller-supplied metadata alone; a forged processing debt, recovery and refund debt refused the same way, with the processing account funded first so the refusal is the guard's and not a lack of balance; no fee, nothing owed. Unit tests cover the leg shape and every refusal, including the internal-field checks and each of the five reserved tags with and without the marker; the largest single chargeback, inquiries excluded; the kind and its write-off; the fee read off balance transactions; the allocation; and, against a stubbed ledger, a consignment split by leg (1125 / 375 of 1500 over 30 / 10), a rising fee per leg, one failing charge not stopping the next, and a cart where one order lacks a split row, or there are none, put on no seller. **Mutation-checked**, each caught by a failing test: posting removed; posting skipped on a refunded order (the first suite missed this, and the after-refund test was added); the whole fee charged to every order on a cart; the partial-dispute rule removed; the sequence removed from the key; the general receivable-tag rule removed (the forged-write test fails); on the unit spec, the dispute-fee-specific internal-field checks removed, a missing split row allowed, and chargebacks summed with inquiries counted. | SD-46 | **A subscription sale never reached its seller or the ledger: no seller link, a card authorized and never captured, and renewals the ledger could not see (F5).** Launch-plan F5 says BMC keeps its 3% on its own sales, and BM-1 recorded that "subscription orders bypass the MercurJS split". Read in full, that was three gaps. (1) A subscription is checked out through Medusa's `completeCartWorkflow`, not Mercur's split (Mercur's refuses a cart without a shipping method per seller, and a vault seat ships nothing), so the order got no Mercur `seller` link. The card ledger settles an order onto that link and refuses one without it (`[Hawala] Card order … has no seller link; not settled`), so no subscription sale ever credited its seller or took the 3%, and the seller's order list never showed it. (2) FBM's Stripe provider authorizes only (`capture` is unset in `medusa-config.ts`, so `capture_method` is manual) and Mercur captures its own carts on `order_set.placed`. Nothing captured a subscription's first order: the card was authorized, the seat delivered and provisioned, and the authorization left to lapse. (3) A live renewal collects with FBM's own off-session PaymentIntent and records it on a `pp_system_default` payment, which the ledger read as "not a card order"; and the PaymentIntent id `renew-helpers.ts` said the session "carries" does not survive — authorization writes the provider's answer over the session's and the payment's `data`, and the system provider answers `{}` (so do its capture and refund). Found on a real database, not by reading. **Done, behind `FF_CONSUMER_SUBSCRIPTIONS_V1`** (`workflows/subscription/steps/subscription-order-settlement.ts`; flag off every step returns before any read, all but the paid step SD-48 added later, which since SD-53 (c) runs with the flag off too): the checkout resolves the cart's one seller before Medusa authorizes the payment session and refuses a cart that has none or several (a card the buyer already confirmed at Stripe, as Blackout's page does before it calls complete, keeps its hold until it lapses); the order is linked to that seller; the card payment is captured (Medusa's `capturePaymentWorkflow`, so the order transaction and `payment.captured` follow) before the subscription is created — a refused capture fails the checkout (the authorization is cancelled, the order deleted and the seller link dismissed; Medusa keeps the cancelled payment on the cart's payment collection), and a failure after the capture deletes the order through `completeCartWorkflow`'s compensation, which then tries to refund the capture (proved when Stripe takes the refund; it is best effort, and a refused refund leaves the card charged with no order and no ledger record — SD-48 open item (b)). SD-48 also found and fixed six gaps in this checkout: a replay of a captured cart whose later step threw refunded the sale while the subscription stayed active; two checkouts of one cart at once were not kept apart; a checkout that failed after the card was authorized could never be completed again on that cart (the capture step counted the cancelled payment Medusa keeps on the collection and refused every retry with "has 2 uncaptured payments", cancelling the new authorization too); a replay made an active subscription from an order its first completion left unlinked and uncaptured; a payment session replaced while the checkout ran let the subscription be made with nothing captured (introduced by SD-48's own fix of the third); and a first completion Medusa's workflow engine left unfinished (SD-53) made the checkout read an order it was not handed, and a retry make an active subscription with no payment at all. The third is F5's own and is on `main` until SD-48 is merged: the same retry, run on a real database against `main`'s checkout sources (c6a463ee), was refused the same way. A renewal order is linked to its seller (logged, not thrown, when no single seller can be found — the money is already collected), its bookkeeping payment is stamped with the PaymentIntent in the payment's `metadata` (no provider call rewrites it and no store route can set it), and, once the charge has `succeeded`, marked captured — no rail is touched. The ledger (`lib/card-order-settlement.ts`) reads such an order as FBM card money only when the order is also linked to the subscription the record names; its refunds are Stripe's figure alone, since a refund recorded in Medusa on a system payment moves no money. Stripe's refund and dispute events on a renewal intent find that payment (`lib/card-stripe-sync.ts`), again only on a verified link, so a copied record is never picked; the capture subscriber reconciles a system-provider capture, and the reconcile decides. Proved on a real migrated database (`integration-tests/http/subscription-order-settlement.spec.ts`, 9 scenarios) with the real `createSubscriptionWorkflow` and live-mode `renewSubscriptionWorkflow`; only the Stripe provider's calls are stubbed on the registered provider, and a renewal's charge is replayed from its recorded result. Deliberate-breakage checks, each run against that spec and each caught by at least one failing scenario (11): no seller link; no first-order capture; no refusal of a multi-seller cart; no link compensation (first passed — the refused-capture scenario read the link through the query graph, which shows nothing for a deleted order; it now reads the link table and the breakage fails it); no renewal stamp; a `processing` renewal recorded as captured; the ledger not checking the subscription link; a Medusa-only refund counted on a renewal; the Stripe sync not checking the link; the capture subscriber ignoring system-provider captures; the flag ignored. Test-harness lesson: a link's `entryPoint`, read by a workflow when it is composed, is `undefined` until the app has registered its links, so a spec that imports such a workflow at the top composes a graph that queries entity `undefined` ("Service \"undefined\" was not found") — the spec requires it after boot; production loads links first. **Open:** (a) digital-product orders (`create-digital-product-order`, used by `/store/carts/:id/complete-digital` and Blackout's one-off listings) have the same two gaps — no seller link, never captured — and are not changed here (closed by SD-48, dark behind `FF_DIGITAL_ORDER_SETTLEMENT_V1`); (b) a renewal still `processing` at the bank is never marked captured later (nothing re-reads the intent once it succeeds; BM-1's ACH item), so it never settles; (c) refund a renewal in the Stripe dashboard, never in Medusa admin: a Medusa refund on its system payment moves no money (the ledger ignores it); (d) the seed scripts list `pp_system_default` on regions — if a production region does, a store client can check out on it without paying (pre-existing; check the live regions). The ledger never reads such an order as card money; (e) no Mercur order set or commission lines for subscription orders: FBM's own 3% in the ledger applies, and Mercur's legacy nightly payout never pays them (it needs a split row) — the ledger payouts (SD-41) do; (f) subscription orders now appear in the seller's vendor-panel order list; whether Mercur's vendor order actions handle an order with no order set is unverified; (g) orders placed before the flag stay unlinked and, if never captured, lapse; a checkout run again on such a cart with the flag on links the order to its products' one seller and captures its authorization if Stripe still holds it, and fails, refunding and delivering nothing new, if Stripe has let it lapse (SD-48; the lapse case by reading Medusa's Stripe provider, which re-throws Stripe's refusal). | done (flag `FF_CONSUMER_SUBSCRIPTIONS_V1`; settles with `FF_CARD_ORDER_LEDGER_V1`); (a) closed by SD-48; (b)-(g) open | `backend/src/workflows/subscription/steps/subscription-order-settlement.ts`, `backend/src/workflows/subscription/workflows/create-subscription.ts`, `backend/src/workflows/subscription/workflows/renew-subscription.ts`, `backend/src/workflows/subscription/renew-helpers.ts`, `backend/src/lib/card-order-settlement.ts`, `backend/src/lib/card-stripe-sync.ts`, `backend/src/subscribers/hawala-card-capture.ts`, `backend/integration-tests/http/subscription-order-settlement.spec.ts` |

One finding on both legs (inferred by rescanning the published images with the 2026-10-11 database: the CI job logs that print the gate's own table are not readable from this environment): `tiff` 4.7.1-r0, `CVE-2026-4775` (HIGH; Red Hat CVSS 7.8; a signed integer overflow in `putcontig8bitYCbCr44tile` gives an out-of-bounds heap write from a crafted TIFF), fixed in 4.7.2-r0, data source the Alpine secdb. **Reproduced on the exact images the gate scanned**, pulled anonymously from GHCR (run with this environment's `GITHUB_TOKEN` withheld: trivy presents it to GHCR, which then answers `DENIED`, possibly what SD-26 hit), with trivy 0.75.0 (what `trivy-action@master` installs by default today; release tarball sha256-checked against its checksums file), the DB of 2026-10-11 01:13 UTC, and the gate's flags (`--severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --ignorefile .trivyignore.image --exit-code 1`): `Total: 1 (HIGH: 1)`, exit 1, for `sha-004eff7` and `sha-7b106a5` of both panels, and for the last green `sha-7b19cc2` as well. **What changed was the advisory data, not the image.** The apk layer has the same diffID in the green and the first red image of each panel (admin `ab83d96e…`, vendor `4a44d031…`: `004eff7` reused the layer `7b19cc2` built at 14:41 UTC with `SECURITY_REFRESH=2026-10-08`); `004eff7` changed six admin-panel source files and nothing in vendor-panel, and vendor-panel went red too. Alpine v3.24 main's secdb records `tiff 4.7.2-r0: CVE-2026-4775`; the secdb file was last modified 2026-10-08 20:37:50 UTC (APKINDEX 20:38:03; the package was built at 11:04). That timestamp is when the whole file last changed, not when the tiff entry first appeared, and the gate does not read secdb: it reads a trivy-db build (rebuilt every six hours, and cached per day by trivy-action), so **the exact moment the advisory reached the gate is not established**. What is established is that the images did not change between the green and the red run (same upgrade-layer diffIDs, above) and that today's database flags the last-green image too. `SECURITY_REFRESH` worked as designed: the 2026-10-11 build re-ran the upgrade layer, which upgrades only what it names. **Why a static-file server has libtiff:** F5's `nginx-module-image-filter` needs `libgd`, which needs `libtiff`; nothing else in the image depends on either. The module is installed but never loaded (the image's `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` has no `load_module`, and neither panel's `nginx.conf` uses `image_filter`), so the flaw is not reachable in the running panels. That lowers the risk; it does not make the finding unfixable, so it is fixed rather than ignored. **A tag bump does not help.** The published images sit on the current `nginx:1.31-alpine` (`sha256:df221db8…`, built 2026-09-22; first eight layers identical), which scans with three HIGH: libexpat and pcre2 (cleared by SD-32's upgrade) and tiff. Every mainline Alpine tag points at that digest; `stable-alpine` also ships tiff 4.7.1-r0 (and would move nginx to 1.30.5); Docker Hub shows no nginx Alpine tag pushed after 2026-09-29, nine days before the fixed tiff was built. **Fixed:** `tiff` joins the scoped list in both panel Dockerfiles (`apk upgrade --no-cache libuuid libexpat pcre2 tiff`), comments updated in lock-step, `SECURITY_REFRESH` still referenced inside the RUN; `.trivyignore.image` untouched. `tiff` is Alpine main: maintainer Michael Mason, origin `tiff`, in the signed v3.24 main APKINDEX, and absent from F5's v3.24 repo (16 packages, all `nginx-packaging@f5.com`). 4.7.2-r0 declares the same dependencies as 4.7.1-r0 and keeps `so:libtiff.so.6`, so the upgrade replaces one package and adds none. **Verified, and how far.** The edited Dockerfiles were **not built**: starting a Docker daemon here was refused. Instead, an offline reconstruction for each panel: the published `sha-7b106a5` image (13 layers, digest-checked) with its apk layer re-packed as the edited RUN writes it, using the real `tiff-4.7.2-r0.apk` (RSA signature verified against the Alpine key in the image's own `/etc/apk/keys`; control hash equals the APKINDEX `C:`; data hash equals `.PKGINFO` `datahash`; both APKINDEXes signature-verified the same way), a whiteout for `libtiff.so.6.2.0`, and `/lib/apk/db/installed` with the tiff record replaced in exactly the shape apk writes (checked against the 4.7.1-r0 record, `Z:` checksums included). Gate flags: **exit 0, 0 findings, 73 packages read, tiff 4.7.2-r0, nginx still 1.31.6-r1**, on both panels. The unmodified control, byte-identical to the published manifest, exits 1 on the tiff finding, so the harness does see it. `pnpm check:panel-feature-flags` passes. As with SD-32, the real proof is the first `main` image scan after the merge. **Open:** (a) Third time (SD-26, SD-32, SD-47) a published Alpine fix has waited for someone to add a package name by hand. The scoping premise, that a bare `apk upgrade` would move nginx off its tag, looks false on the current base: `/etc/apk/repositories` lists only Alpine main and community (the base installs F5's packages with `apk add -X https://nginx.org/...` and never persists that repo), and `/etc/apk/world` pins `nginx=1.31.6-r1` and every module with `=`. Untested by a real build; worth one (bare `apk upgrade`, then `apk info -v` on nginx and its modules) before the list grows again. (b) `nginx:1.31-alpine-slim` carries the same nginx 1.31.6-r1 with 21 packages instead of 73 and none of tiff, libgd, libxml2 or libxslt; its only HIGH today is pcre2, which the list already clears. Since neither panel loads a dynamic module, it would remove most of the surface this class keeps hitting. Not done: it changes the base variant and needs a real build and a smoke test. (c) Six more installed Alpine packages trail the index without tripping the gate: `libpng` (CVE-2026-46675), `nghttp2-libs` (CVE-2026-58055) and `zlib` (CVE-2026-85091), all MEDIUM; `libcrypto3`/`libssl3` 3.5.8-r0 to 3.5.9-r0 (no secdb entry yet); `tzdata`. Not added: the list has held only what the gate needs. (d) `CLAUDE.md`'s Docker paragraph still says the upgrade is "scoped to libuuid", stale since SD-32. | SD-48 | **A digital-product sale never reached its seller or the ledger: no seller link, and a card authorized and never captured (SD-46 open item (a)).** `create-digital-product-order` serves `POST /store/carts/:id/complete-digital`, `/v1/checkout/sessions/:id/page` (`?action=complete` and POST) and Blackout's one-off listing checkout — the one live caller; no first-party client calls the other two — and completes the cart with Medusa's `completeCartWorkflow`, not Mercur's split. **Seen on a real migrated database before any change:** a probe (not kept) ran the real workflow over six cart shapes with only the Stripe provider stubbed, then let the in-app subscribers run. No completed order had a `seller_seller_order_order` row, and every completed order's `pp_stripe_stripe` payment stayed authorized (`captured_amount` 0, no provider capture call). Nothing captures it later: Mercur's only capture subscriber listens to `order_set.placed`, which this workflow never emits, and no FBM subscriber, job or flow captures one of these payments (FBM's only captures are F5's, inside the subscription workflows) — only the admin panel's manual capture button on the order page could. So the card ledger refuses the order (no seller link), the seller is never credited, BMC's 3% is never taken, and the authorization lapses. The probe also showed a cart holding two sellers' products completing into one unlinked order, and a product with no seller link completing too; every digital product created through `POST /admin/digital-products` has none, since nothing in that flow links one (the vendor panel's digital-products page calls the same admin route). **Done, behind new `FF_DIGITAL_ORDER_SETTLEMENT_V1`** (default off, backend only; settles with `FF_CARD_ORDER_LEDGER_V1`): the workflow runs F5's own step functions, not copies, as its own `*DigitalProduct*` steps with the sale fixed to `digital_product` (`workflows/subscription/steps/subscription-order-settlement.ts`; each sale reads only its own flag, and F5's subscription wording is unchanged). After the cart lock is taken and before Medusa authorizes any payment session, the cart's one seller is resolved and a cart with none or several is refused (the store route answers 400). Medusa then authorizes nothing, so nothing is captured; a card the buyer already confirmed with Stripe — Blackout's page runs `stripe.confirmPayment` before it calls complete — keeps its uncaptured hold until it lapses, as on any refused completion. The order is linked to that seller, and the card is captured with Medusa's `capturePaymentWorkflow` before the digital product order is created. A capture Stripe refuses fails the checkout — the authorization is cancelled (Medusa keeps the cancelled payment on the cart's payment collection), `completeCartWorkflow`'s compensation deletes the order, the seller link is dismissed, and no digital product order is created; since point (10) below, a retry with a new payment session then completes normally. A failure after the capture deletes the order the same way, and that compensation then tries to refund the capture (`compensatePaymentIfNeededStep`) — best effort, open item (b). A payment Stripe already captured at authorization (session data a store client can set to `capture_method: automatic`) is not captured again. **Flag off, byte-identical:** every new step returns before any read (unit-tested per step and per flag, with either flag on alone), and the same probe on this branch with the flag off gave a normalized snapshot identical to main's for all six shapes — every row of every table with an `order_id` column, the order, its transactions and fulfillments, the payment collection, sessions, payments, captures and refunds, the Stripe calls, the events emitted, and the ledger legs (random ids and fixture names masked, and the order of two link events one parallel step emits, which varies on main too). Re-checked after the repair with the reviewers' flag-off probe, both flags off, ten cart shapes per side (the six above, a replay of each checkout, and a replay of each checkout's cart after an admin captured its payment, with the order read failing once): this branch's sources (6b3572cc) and the merge base's (7b106a5b) for the five files SD-48 changes gave identical masked snapshots for all ten. The base side hung twice in the test runner's teardown (a nested `complete-cart` checkpoint left `invoking`, as in the harness lesson below) and passed on its third run. Identical includes the admin-captured replay: on main and here alike it refunds the captured 5 while the order stays (open item (j)). **Proved on a real migrated database** (`integration-tests/http/digital-order-settlement.spec.ts`, 27 scenarios, 10 of them from the first pass): a Blackout one-off listing's order linked, captured once, and settled to its seller less exactly 3% (15 of 500 cents); a digital product's order captured before its digital product order exists (by call order), then linked, fulfilled and settled; a payment Stripe already captured not captured again (no capture workflow runs at all); a two-seller cart and a product with no seller refused before `authorizePayment`; the store route's 400; a refused capture leaving no order and no live row in the seller-order link table (read directly), and the cart's lock free again; a failure after the capture refunded when Stripe takes the refund; flag off unchanged even with `FF_CONSUMER_SUBSCRIPTIONS_V1` on, and a two-seller cart still completing as before. The other 17, and the subscription spec's (22 scenarios), are listed under the two reviews below. **Deliberate-breakage checks of the first pass** (13, each run against that spec and the step unit spec, each caught by at least one failing test): no seller link (3 scenarios); no capture (4); the seller resolved after authorization (3); the capture after the digital product order is created (3); no link compensation (2, both reading the link table); the flag ignored (the 2 flag-off scenarios, 6 unit); the digital sale gated by the subscription flag (9, 4 unit); the subscription sale also enabled by the digital flag (3 unit); a read before the flag check (3 unit); an already-captured payment captured again (first passed: Medusa makes a second capture a no-op at the provider and dedupes the order transaction, so nothing the scenario read changed; it now counts `payment.captured` per payment, and the breakage fails it); the no-seller reason dropped (1); the several-sellers check dropped (2, 2 unit); a step with no `sale` defaulting to the digital flag (4 unit). Test-harness lesson: the runner's teardown waits only for stored workflow executions, while in-app subscribers set off by a checkout's events keep running after a test ends. Once (in 1 of 13 breakage runs; its re-run completed), a test failing straight after a checkout let the runner truncate the database under them, and the next test's nested `complete-cart` stayed `waiting_to_compensate` with `create-remote-links` and `update-carts` never answering; `waitWorkflowExecutions` then polled for over 15 minutes. Later breakage runs were guarded by a timeout. **Review and repair (2026-10-11).** Two reviews of the first pass found one major gap and eight minor ones, and a double submit was added to them; each gap was seen on a real database before anything changed. (1) *A replay refunded a delivered sale (major; both checkouts).* Run again on a cart it had already completed — a retried store call, a refreshed `/v1/checkout/sessions/:token/page?action=complete` (the session mint takes any cart id, without authentication), Blackout's "retry finishes the record" — either checkout re-entered `completeCartWorkflow`. On a completed cart that creates nothing, but it still registers `compensatePaymentIfNeededStep` outside its create-order branch, and that compensation refunds the cart's payment whenever `captured_at` is set; so with either flag on, any throw after it refunded the whole sale while the order, its seller link and what it delivered stayed. Seen with the product moved to another seller since the sale (the link step refuses that): 5 of 5 refunded for both sales, the subscription left `active`, and (digital sale, `FF_CARD_ORDER_LEDGER_V1` on) the refund subscriber reversing the seller's 485 and BMC's 15; for the digital sale also with one transient read failure, and over the store route (a second POST answered 400 after refunding). Fix: with its flag on, each checkout first reads the cart's `order_cart` link (the signal `completeCartWorkflow` itself uses) and runs `completeCartWorkflow` and the seller, link and capture steps only for a cart not yet completed; a replay returns the order as its first completion left it, and links, captures, refuses and refunds nothing. Flag off, the read is skipped and a replay goes through `completeCartWorkflow` as on main. The digital steps also became their own `createStep` definitions instead of F5's steps renamed with `.config({ name })`: inside a `when` block workflows-sdk 2.14.2 re-registers the handler built under the step's first name (`refRet.if` in `create-step.js`), whose compensation looks the result up under that name, finds nothing and does nothing — the first run of the fix left the seller link behind a refused capture until this was found. Scenarios: a plain replay (one capture, no refund, one digital product order or subscription), a replay after the product moved seller (nothing refunded; the ledger legs unchanged), a replay whose later read fails once (nothing refunded), and for the digital sale a replay after the product lost its seller, a retried POST over the store route (200, same order), and a flag-off replay. (2) *A double submit (added by the coordinator).* Two checkouts of one cart at once, probed at three timings: the digital checkout was already serialised — it has held the cart-id lock from its first step to its last since before SD-48, and `completeCartWorkflow`, nested through `runAsStep`, skips its own acquire and release (`StepResponse.skip()` when `parentStepIdempotencyKey` is set, which `runAsStep` sets) — so the second run was refused the lock by Medusa's in-memory provider, retried every 0.3 s, then replayed: one order, one capture, no refund, one digital product order, also over the store route. The subscription checkout held no lock at all, and every timing went wrong: with no delay, two orders on one cart and one payment collection, two subscriptions, two seller links and two capture rows on one payment (Stripe's capture called twice); with a slow capture, the run that lost the race to record the payment failed (`Payment with payment_session_id … already exists` — the payment module's `authorizePaymentSession` checks, then writes) after the payment module had sent Stripe a cancel for the PaymentIntent the other run then captured (the stub accepted both calls; against Stripe, cancelling an uncaptured PaymentIntent releases the hold — not run against Stripe); with a slow authorization, the losing run's compensation refunded the winner's capture in full ("Refunded due to cart completion failure") while the winner's subscription stayed active. Fix: flag on, the subscription checkout locks the cart id from its first step to its last (`subscriptionCheckoutLockStep` gives the key; Medusa's `acquireLockStep`, 30 s timeout and 120 s ttl, whose compensation releases it on failure, and `releaseLockStep` at the end); flag off it gets no key and takes no lock, as on main. The coordinator suggested a key different from `completeCartWorkflow`'s so that the two could not deadlock. They cannot meet on the same key either, since the nested acquire and release are skipped, and the bare cart id is what the digital, ticket and rental checkouts and Medusa's own cart workflows lock, so it also keeps a cart edit, a digital checkout or a top-level completion of the same cart out of a subscription checkout in progress, which a prefixed key would not (read from the in-memory provider, which keys locks by string; not run as a scenario). After the fix the same probe gave one order, one capture, no refund and one subscription at all three timings. Scenarios, both sales: two runs at once and two POSTs at once (`POST /store/subscriptions` with a customer token; `POST /store/carts/:id/complete-digital`) give one order, one capture, nothing refunded or cancelled, and one subscription or digital product order; the two-runs scenarios also read that one run was refused the lock at least once, each run took it once, and the seller was checked once (the second replayed) — the two-POSTs scenarios read neither; a second checkout kept waiting past 30 s fails at `acquire-lock-step` before any money step, without freeing the lock it never held, and the cart then checks out normally; after a refused capture the cart's lock is free at once; flag off, the subscription checkout never calls the locking module. (3) *The link step's refusal was untested:* changing its `mode: "initial"` to `"renewal"` (log instead of throw) left every scenario green, because the seller check always refused first. New scenario per sale: the product moves to another seller while Stripe authorizes the card, after the seller check; the link step refuses ("… is sold by B, not A as checked before payment"), the authorization is cancelled, nothing is captured or refunded, and no order, seller link, subscription or digital product order remains. (4) *The late refund was stated without its condition* — here, in `feature-flags.ts`, in both checkouts' comments and in SD-46. It now says best effort everywhere (open item (b)). (5) *Orders completed before the flag:* at 93316983 a flag-on replay of one linked it and captured its old authorization (seen on a real database; by reading, an expired authorization would have made such a replay fail). The replay fix removed both; the second review found that this also let a replay deliver an order its first completion left unfinished, and since point (11) a replay links and captures such an order again (open item (d)). (6) *`ensureListingProduct` left a seller-less shadow product seller-less:* its handle-recovery path (a product an earlier run created and never recorded) and its early return for a listing that already carries `product_id` never linked the seller, so every flag-on purchase of such a product was refused. Both now call the same `linkSeller` as creation, so the link is tried again on every render and completion of the Blackout page. On a real database Medusa's link module takes the same seller–product pair again without error (its repository upserts and clears `deleted_at`), restores a dismissed link, and refuses a product another seller holds (`Cannot create multiple links between 'seller' and 'product'`, which `linkSeller` logs and leaves alone); the repaired product then checks out to the listing's seller. Unit-tested per path. (7) and (8) became open items (g)-(i). (9) The flag comment, the subscription and digital workflows' comments and the Blackout contract note now say the seller check precedes Medusa's `authorizePaymentSession`, not the card authorization (the first commit's message, 7a786234, still says "before any payment is authorized"). **Deliberate-breakage checks of the repair** (18, each run against the named real-database scenarios or unit tests, the sources restored from git after each; every one caught): the replay read ignored (digital: 5 scenarios fail; subscription: 3); each checkout's replay gate always taking the first-completion path (5; 3); no subscription lock (all 3 double-submit scenarios); the lock taken after the replay check (1: the two-runs scenario's seller count; the two-POSTs scenario passed); the lock released straight after the replay check (1: the two-POSTs scenario; the two-runs one passed on timing, as the second run polls every 0.3 s and by then the first had made its order); the lock taken without its releasing compensation (the refused-capture scenario's lock check, each sale); a 1 s lock timeout (the 30 s scenario, each sale); the subscription lock ignoring its flag (the flag-off scenario, 2 unit) or reading the digital flag (2 unit); the digital lock removed (all 3 double-submit scenarios); the link step's `initial` mode changed to `renewal` (the link-refusal scenario, each sale); `ensureListingProduct`'s early-return link removed (the real-database scenario, 2 unit) and its recovery-path link removed (1 unit). Probes and mutations were scratch files, never committed. **Second review and repair (2026-10-11).** A fresh review of the repair found two more gaps and three nits, each reproduced on a real database before anything changed. (10) *A checkout that failed after the card was authorized could never be completed again on that cart (both checkouts; F5's capture selection, so on `main` too).* `completeCartWorkflow`'s compensation cancels the payment, and Medusa keeps the cancelled payment on the cart's payment collection. A retry pays with a new payment session (`createPaymentSessionsWorkflow` deletes the collection's sessions first, as the storefront does when the buyer pays again), but the capture step counted every uncaptured FBM payment on the order and refused with "has 2 uncaptured payments; none captured"; each refusal cancelled the new authorization too, so the next retry saw three. Seen after a capture Stripe refused and after one transient read failure in the link step, for both sales; the same probe against `main`'s three checkout sources (c6a463ee) was refused the same way for the subscription checkout; with the flag off, the reviewer saw the same retry succeed. Fix: the step considers only payments whose payment session the collection still has, and the earlier attempt's payment has none. The sessions are read in a query of their own: asked for as `payments.payment_session.id`, the order query drops a payment whose session is gone (seen on a real database), which would hide the rule inside the read. A cancelled payment on the cart's current session stays the one to capture, and the payment module refuses it: that is a retry on the same session, which `authorizePaymentSession` answers with the payment it already has. Ignoring cancelled payments instead, as the review suggested, let that retry complete with no errors although its only payment was the cancelled one (seen on a real database for both sales). (11) *A replay delivered an order its first completion left unfinished (both checkouts; introduced by point (1)).* The replay gate skipped the link and the capture whenever the cart had an order, and the steps after it still delivered: a digital product order created and fulfilled, an active subscription. A first completion that stops right after `completeCartWorkflow` (a restart or deploy mid-checkout, or Medusa's Stripe webhook, open item (g)) leaves exactly that order, authorized and unlinked, and the retry delivered it unlinked and uncaptured (seen for both sales and for a Blackout one-off listing's cart shape; that page then grants the listing's `feature_keys`, by reading the route). Fix: the link and capture steps run on a replay too, still outside `completeCartWorkflow`. The link step's `replay` mode leaves a linked order as it is, whatever its product's seller is now, links an unlinked one to its products' one seller, and never throws. The capture step's `replay` mode captures the order's authorized, uncaptured FBM payment on the cart's current session once the order is linked, and captures nothing for an order it could not link (no seller could be credited), logging `… has no seller link, so this checkout captures nothing for it`. A refused capture fails the retry before anything is delivered; nothing refunds anything, and the retry's own seller link is dismissed by its compensation. A first completion runs as before; flag off, every step still returns before any read. (12) SD-46 said the subscription seller check comes "before any payment is authorized"; it now says Medusa's `authorizePaymentSession`, as this row and the code do. (13) The double-submit sentence above credited the lock and seller-check counts to the two-POSTs scenarios too; only the two-runs scenarios read them. (14) The subscription spec had no flag-off replay scenario; it has one now (same order, unlinked and uncaptured, one subscription, the locking module never called). "Nothing left behind" after a refused capture is corrected here, in SD-46, in `feature-flags.ts` and in the digital checkout's comment. The first version (`76249690`) did not: it waited in the suite's own `afterEach`, and the runner declares its `afterEach` (wait for executions, then truncate) in the same block first, while Jest runs one block's `afterEach` hooks in declaration order, so the drain ran after the truncate. (16) *A payment session replaced while the checkout ran let the order through uncaptured (both checkouts; introduced by point (10)).* The store's payment-collection route lets a client open a new session at any time, and Medusa then cancels the old intent at Stripe. Point (10)'s rule considered only payments whose session the collection still has, so the authorized payment dropped out, nothing was captured and the order was delivered, with no error at all (seen on a real database for both sales). Now the only payment passed over is an earlier attempt's leftover, cancelled and with its session gone; the replaced session's payment stays the one to capture, Stripe refuses it, and nothing is delivered. The second repair's fixer found and wrote this before its session ended; it was applied and verified here. The order stays, because Medusa's compensation of the stopped run never finishes, so a retry finds it as a replay, and with nothing to capture the replay delivered it: the digital product order made, the subscription active, no payment at all (reproduced on demand for both sales). That was a reading of the code. Two independent reviews ran the endpoint on a real database, and their runs were reproduced. *As written,* `GET /vendor/plant-nursery/payouts/current-period` multiplies sales by `getGrowerTier().current_split_pct` (`current-period/route.ts:90`, `:115`, `:158-159`, `:168`, `:176-177`) with no platform fee subtracted, and backs the nursery portal's Payouts page and its dashboard's "{n}% split". Three faults. The first alone explains everything observed; the second and third each zero a different part of the money figures even for the right id (the order read gives units sold and "your cut", the ledger read gives gross, net, the monthly history and year-to-date), and neither touches the tier or split, which come only from the tier read: (1) the grower is looked up by `getSellerId` (`backend/src/api/vendor/quests/_helpers.ts:6-9`), which returns `auth_context.actor_id`, the member id: Mercur's `createSellerWorkflow` links the auth identity to the member, and `ensureSellerContext` rewrites a seller-id actor to the member id, so the tier, order and ledger reads find no seller, KARMA, plan or account; (2) the order read (`getSellerOrders`) fails on Medusa 2.14.2 and returns `[]` for any id (SD-52); (3) the ledger figures read only PURCHASE credits on SELLER_EARNINGS, which no settlement writes (the seller leg is TRANSFER), so they would read 0 for the right account too (a reading of the code, not run). `GET /vendor/farm/grower-dashboard` has fault (1): it reads `auth_context.actor_id`, so its `karma` is Seedling at 0.6 for everyone. Both endpoints also write on a read (SD-51). Faults (1) and (2) are in code, not data, so production should behave the same; production was not observed. **What growers were shown,** so far as this repository shows: never a tier-scaled amount of their own sales; 60% and zeros, to anyone who opened those screens (the portals are not deployed by this repository). The route and both helpers are unchanged since 2026-07-11, the actor rewrite was already registered on `/vendor/**`, and Medusa was pinned at 2.14.2 then as now (GitHub history, not run on the July code). The public `/karma` page publishes the ladder as what each tier pays. **Not fixed here:** F7 step 1 changes no behaviour, and the right figure (the seller leg if there is no hub cut, or a flat share) is the operator's F7 decision (inventory §10). A production database built by these migrations has the fault; one whose schema came from elsewhere may not, and production's schema is not visible from here. **Not fixed here:** F7 step 1 changes no behaviour. Without that patch (`backend/scripts/patch-mikro-orm.js:105-113`) the same read fails earlier, before any SQL, with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'kind')" (also observed). Ten other files under `backend/src` mention `items.quantity`; some read carts, where the field exists; they were not checked. **Not fixed here:** F7 step 1 changes no behaviour. The fix is to read `items.*` instead, with a real-database spec per caller. For the grower and wellness KARMA subscribers, that starts awarding KARMA for sales, which bears on F7 (SD-49, SD-50; inventory §10.8); for the wellness subscriber it also starts registering class and membership buyers. **Fixed on branch `fix/p0-sd52-items-quantity` (2026-11-15; not merged).** Eight order reads select `items.*` instead: the cottage-food meter, the Blackout `order.placed` emitter, the wellness subscriber, `getSellerOrders`, seller push, the customer data export, Black Mask provisioning and the grower dashboard. Where a fixed read starts producing money it converts Medusa's major units to the cents its consumer documents (the meter, `seller_total_cents`, the grower dashboard's revenue, `order.created`'s prices). `backend/src/shared/__tests__/order-items-quantity-guard.unit.spec.ts` fails on any order read naming an `items.<field>` OrderLineItem lacks (`items.total` fails the same way as `items.quantity`, and `items.totals_id` too). Fixing the reads switched on code that had never run, and the reviews found what it did wrong. Each is fixed on the branch and has a case in `backend/integration-tests/http/order-items-quantity-read.spec.ts`, which runs on a migrated database. (a) The Blackout `order.created`, `order.updated` and `order.cancelled` events went to vendorId "default-seller": Order has no `seller_id`, so the field read as absent. They now route by Mercur's `seller.id` link. `purchase.succeeded` goes out only for Blackout catalog lines, and the buyer's Blackout id is never the seller's. (b) Wellness takes one seat per ticket, is safe to redeliver, and sends "You're registered" only when a seat was taken. (c) `getSellerOrders` takes `since`, applied in the database. *The final review found two more.* (d) The wellness subscriber called `registerForClass` for every class linked to the ticket's product, whatever its status or date, and `registerForClass` wrote `status: "open"` back onto the class. The vendor DELETE soft-cancels a class and leaves its product linked, so a ticket bought after a cancellation reopened the class, seated the buyer and said they were registered. A class that ended last month took a seat the same way, and one drop-in ticket took a seat in every session sharing its product. Now the subscriber reads only live, future classes, filtered in the database: status in `LIVE_CLASS_STATUSES` (scheduled, open, full: the set the hourly reminder job uses, which now imports the same constant) and `ends_at` later than now. A product with several such classes seats nobody and logs a warning, unless the line's `metadata.class_event_id` names one of that product's live classes. No first-party client sends that field (`storefront/src` has no `class_event_id`), and a value naming a dead class or another product's class seats nobody. The service layer is guarded too: `registerForClass` refuses a cancelled, completed or otherwise non-live class, and one whose `ends_at` has passed. It refuses before any write and returns `refused` (`backend/src/modules/wellness/class-registration.ts`). The subscriber logs that and sends no message. The vendor's manual add, which also seated an attendee in a cancelled or ended class and reopened it, now answers 409 with the reason. (e) `getSellerOrders` had no status filter, so once its read worked it listed cancelled and draft orders, and `GET /vendor/revenue/channels` counted each one as an FBM sale with the 3% fee on it. The read now filters on three conditions: `status` not canceled or draft, `canceled_at` null, and `is_draft_order` false. Checked on Postgres through query.graph: each condition filters in the database, and none is enough alone. Medusa's archive moves a cancelled order or a draft to status "archived" and keeps `canceled_at` and `is_draft_order`, so `status` alone keeps both. A draft is never cancelled, so `canceled_at` alone keeps drafts. Medusa's and Mercur's cancels both set `canceled_at`, so for orders they write, `status` adds only a hand-written status. *Mutation checks* (each change reverted, the matching tests watched fail, then restored): with no subscriber filter, a ticket for the live session beside a cancelled one and an ended one seats nobody; with no service guard, `registerForClass` seats a buyer in a cancelled or ended class and in a class cancelled mid-registration; with neither, the subscriber seats the buyer in the cancelled class and in last month's class (the original bug); with no ambiguity check, a ticket takes a seat with two live sessions; with `class_event_id` ignored, both pinning cases fail; with no handling of `refused`, the warning is missing; dropping any one seller-filter condition lists a non-sale. **Still open:** `plant-order-helpers.ts` (the grower KARMA read) and wellness sale KARMA (`FF_WELLNESS_SALE_KARMA_V1`, default off) wait on the operator under F7 inventory §10 item 8. `shared/order-dispute-intake.ts` still selects `items.total`, so no buyer can open a dispute on a real order; that needs its own change, because the units and the seller path need fixing too. A paid ticket that takes no seat is only logged, with no buyer or vendor notification and no refund. That covers a class that is full with no waitlist, a class that is cancelled, completed or over, and a shared product whose line names no class. The vendor DELETE leaves a cancelled class's product on sale, and nothing marks a class completed when it ends. Until a client sends `class_event_id`, a product shared by several live sessions seats nobody. A vendor can no longer add an attendee to a class that has ended (409). `registerForClass` counts seats with a read and then a write, with no lock, so two orders at once can both take the last seat. That was already true of the manual add; it can now happen from order.placed too. The nursery dashboard and payouts routes still call `getSellerOrders` without `since`. | re-review follow-ups (cross-seller class/tier linking, reminders, message tokens, payout cents, grower dashboard) fixed in SD-81; fixed (`3b0f58a` … `176ae82` on `claude/intelligent-mayer-7zymwu`, from `fix/p0-sd52-items-quantity`), including the final review's two items; the dispute intake (`items.total`) was fixed by SD-79; open: the operator-gated grower and wellness sale KARMA (F7 §10 item 8) and the follow-ups under **Still open**.
